comments.body: A person I'd cared for and loved for 30 years, had to take hospice at home. He was much older than me, and we were both retired in different states.  His family was happy to have me travel across several states to stay with him and care, clean and feed him for several months before he died. Unknown to me, he had another lover that the family conspired to keep me in the dark about. They would invent day trips to get me away when she came to visit. He was not in any condition to have physical relations with anybody of course. However, I found out who and what she was. In his confused state, he asked me to read and send text and Whatsapp messages for him.  That is how I found out their relationship coincided with the time of my relationship with him. I was devastated. I came to believe that the family used me instead of paying someone to be with him full time, which he required. Obviously I was much cheaper than a paid health care worker. They did pay for 2 out of my 4 round trip flights. I had my own house and tasks that required me to go home on occasion. I am not poor, I paid for all my expenses & needs along with buying expensive items to make him more comfortable.When I found all this out, all I wanted to do was go home and leave him to his fate. He died a few days after I left. This story is simply to illustrate the lengths that people will or must do, just to get the kind of care necessary to die in this country.

We have a massively dysfunctional healthcare system.  It’s grossly inefficient while being extraordinarily expensive.  Those of us with loved ones suffering from dementia are canaries in the coal mine.  The impact is unavoidable.  

Even “quality” long term care places are short staffed.  Two shifts, not three, means long hours for already overburdened people.  Have said it before and will say it again, the people doing the hands on work are wage slaves.  

Continuity in care tends to be missing and those with dementia are rarely in a position to advocate for themselves so family involvement and monitoring are key to keeping cognitive functioning from deteriorating at a faster pace.  Same goes for physical health.  Those without family or concerned friends get overlooked in ways that are appalling.  

There’s no chance that the state of affairs for us will improve while Republicans are in power.  They’re largely responsible for all the pigs at the trough and as one might expect, none of the piggies are interested in any measures which reduce their gluttonous consumption of resources.  

And the struggle for accountability is constant.  It’s hard to avoid being adversarial under such circumstances.  Remember though, many places are for profit.  That’s the whole problem in a nutshell.

We had five needy aging parents all at the same time (parents and step parent) and none lived in our state. At the same time we were sending our kid to college, while working full time. One sister was able to step up on site to help mom who had dementia and dad who had his faculties but his body was breaking down. Step mother had full blown Alzheimers and husband’s dad was in denial. His mom was the only one who had planned for long term care but even then, she required significant care and involvement from us.  Between 2010-2020 we lost them all but had spent tens of thousands shuttling across the country, from one to another, to offer the care we could and didn’t vacation for a decade. Coupled with college tuition, retirement savings definitely took a back seat. 

Now our older sister requires care which is divided among three other siblings and her daughter who lives abroad. Yes, it’s a squeeze. Yes, the one sister who cared for parents still harbors resentment (though she got the bulk of their estate) and now only grudgingly helps with sis, and yes, it’s wearing and lonely and expensive to meet family obligations. Most American families are alone in this process and it would be a huge benefit if we could all get help because without it we are all breaking the bank.

After retiring during the pandemic,  we began researching and visiting all sorts of retirement living communities within the surrounding five states. 
Took us 18 months to realize we prefer nonprofit Life Plan Communitites with cottages vs apartments or large homes, walking trails, and highly engaged residents. We became used to the idea that you have to pay for good future care,  including social workers,  on-site medical clinics, and good contracts.  Both communities we're waitlisted at must have 2 residents on their governing boards.
Because we have no heirs, and are able to move while still fit and able to make new friends and fully embrace the community, and will require access to all services and care as we become decrepit, we plan to move in as soon as we meet the waiting requirements of between 3 and 8 years, depending on the size abd availability of out new home.
We're grateful for the existence of Life Plan Communities.
You, and/or your elders should investigate these communities ASAP.

A few thoughts:
1. I have 2 family members who've been on these drugs, life changing for both. For one, quieting a lifetime of "food noise," improved a1C and cardio markers, no knee pain, and feeling better about himself than he has in decades. For the other, hopefully helping her avoid the health consequences from much of the same genetic profile, and helping her get to and maintain a weight where she feels confident. (She is an aspiring actor, so of course the issues in that industry are a challenge for most anyone!). That said, she's had trouble eating enough to maintain her energy - this seems like a real downside of these meds. Next up we need meds to help boost metabolism for people like my relative.
2. Restaurants are starting to have smaller portions b/c so many people are on GLP-1 meds; maybe there will be societal benefits all around as food options become healthier.
3. The cult of "thinness" is indeed a plague but standards of attractiveness are not immutable. Trends come & go, different cultures have different standards. If you're in a culture that values thinness, you can't reprogram the libido/desire of everyone to reject that idea. It's a deeply complex phenomenon. My own sense of whether I look good (attractive) is ingrained over 60 years, I can't just tell myself to get over it if my rational brain disagrees with my lizard brain.

I have had psoriasis plaque on my body since I was 17 years old. Mostly my elbows, knees, and ankles. During eras of high stress and poor health (like mono and untreated autoimmune thyroid disease), plaque has also covered my scalp, inside my ears, my knuckles, my shins, and forearms. I had to quit playing fretted instruments because I couldn’t form calluses that wouldn’t perpetually scale off. My nails and fingers and toes looked geriatric by my late 30s. And full-blown psoriatic arthritis is a debilitating condition. 

At 62, a year into glp-1 treatment, I am six months into plaque-free living for the first time since 1980.   I haven’t picked up a guitar, I’m not tempting triggers, and scars and misshapen digits are forever. But this kind of essay is a deep threat to a wellbeing I thought I would never know again. 

I started to address a BMI of 29, a scale that wouldn’t budge despite the resources and information to eat healthy, but I’m staying for the anti-inflammatory properties that have markedly improved my quality of life with a lower side effect profile than before imaginable. My weight is now in the normal range exactly where I want it and after a half century of yo-yo’ing the same 50 lbs, it can stay. 

Quit vilifying an unimaginable leap forward in metabolic health with a low side effect profile. Instead focus on driving down cost and increasing access. Good lord, how do you have to be told? I knew the for-profit industry never actually cared about prevention.

comments.name: Daniel
comments.body: I recently started reading "Natural Habitats and Wildlife Gardening" by Shaun McCoshum, published this year by Princeton University Press. It makes a compelling case that often, what is missing from backyard ecosystems is not just "food" (coming primarily from flowering plants), but places for insects and other animals to nest, breed, and overwinter. The book is filled with useful suggestions on ways to enhance soil diversity, provide burrows, dead wood/organic matter, rocks, water, and other structures that can be used by wildlife for all purposes. Great lessons in here for those interested in doing their part to help local wildlife, and a good reminder that the factors that matter to other species are much more complex than just native versus nonnative plants!

There are quite a few variety of milkweed plants out there but there's one in particular called tropical milkweed that is sold everywhere. Even that comes in 2 colors and maybe more.  Over the years I planted different types including many natives.  Even having two plants side by side, it was clear that the monarchs preferred that tropical milkweed and specifically in orange.  It was where you found their eggs and of course the caterpillars. Now that plant has a bad rap as it can spread EO, a bad and deadly pathogen.  That's mainly because it doesn't die back in winter in warm states/areas.  I learned how to keep it and keep the butterflies safe by not letting it seed, to cut it back yourself and dig up and treat the soil beneath it.  As soon as I saw natives in this article I instantly thought about milkweed.

Reading that more Americans than ever are taking weight-loss medications really resonated with me because I am one of those success stories. Seven weeks ago, I weighed 302 pounds. Today, I weigh 264 pounds—a loss of 38 pounds in less than two months while taking Zepbound.

  Like many people struggling with obesity, I spent years trying different approaches. I learned that weight loss is not simply about willpower. It involves biology, metabolism, hormones, habits, stress, sleep, and countless other factors. For some of us, medications such as Zepbound help address the biological side of the equation in a way that diet and exercise alone could not.

 What has surprised me most is that the medication is not a magic solution. It is a tool. I still have to make better food choices, stay hydrated, remain active, and be mindful of long-term habits. The difference is that I no longer feel like I am fighting my own body every step of the way.

  Beyond the physical changes, I have noticed improvements in energy, mobility, confidence, and overall quality of life. Everyday tasks are easier, and I feel more motivated to continue improving my health.

  My journey is far from over, but going from 302 pounds to 264 pounds in seven weeks has shown me that meaningful change is possible.

And I’m ashamed to admit that despite the vet’s heads up about the likely side effects, I was woefully unprepared and completely caught off guard. He peed in my apartment building’s elevator, hallways, lobby, etc, nearly every time we took a bathroom break — to the point where I started bringing a tote full of paper towels & disinfectant around with me. But even then, keeping up with him and the cleaning was difficult. I’m sure my neighbors abhorred me. And of course, by the time the doggie diapers I ordered for him arrived, he’d finished his course of meds and was back to his usual self. Thank goodness!

But this is all to say: an elderly dog’s incontinence (and owner’s failure to appropriately cleanup after it), though unsanitary, does NOT necessarily equate animal abuse. I’d advise against jumping to conclusions.

At least in the US (I can't say for UK, FR, GER) the standard of living for the poor, and for the rich, has been *increasing*.   This is very visible, and further irritates the middle class.  The primary causes - automation, communication technology, and now AI - are only going to make these problems worse.

While immigration is not a primary driver of these economic changes, the reality is that humans are deeply tribal, and, if they are already irritated, going out and seeing a lot of people who don't look like them makes them even more irritated.

Finally, 90 years ago, government spending was 2% of GDP, so making some minor moves towards socialism (e.g. Social Security) could be made relatively cheaply.  Now with government spending well about 20% of GDP, getting taxed even more for income redistribution is politically not viable.

The far-right can't solve these problems any more than the center or the left.  They understand this, and their strategy is to give people someone to BLAME.  This is very comforting to the angry masses, even if in reality nothing is being done to fix things.

I was lucky enough to work somewhere that still had a fax machine in 2012/2013. comments.body:
Some readers wonder why Le Pen is running for the 4th time when she has failed 3 times already. 

French politics work differently than the American version.

In France it is not unheard of to run and fail a couple of times before being elected President. Mitterrand was elected President on the *third* try (1965, 1974, 1981). Chirac as well (1981, 1988, 1995). They both went on to win reelection (Mitterrand in 1988 and Chirac in 2002). 

Legal problems aside, there is nothing strange about Le Pen running again. Especially since her party has gone from a fringe phenomenon to now being the most popular in France. Marine Le Pen herself has seen her score go up with every try: in 2012 she got 18% in the first round and was eliminated; in 2017 she got 21% in the first round and went on to get 34% in the second round; in 2022 she got 23% in the first round and 41.5% in the second round.  

Given this linear progression, her huge popularity, and historical precedent, she has every reason to believe she can clutch victory this time. Which obviously doesn't mean she will, but in her universe it makes sense to try again.

He must stand on his own, sell the public he is the better person for France.

She lost three times.  What makes her believe that this time she will succeed?
France has a huge problem with entitlements.  And French people are extremely resistant about giving any of these entitlements up.
She’s like Trump saying that Obamacare is bad and that only he can repeal it and offer a cheaper and better alternative.
We’re still waiting!  And I think LePen/Bardella are copying the Trump playbook.  Are there enough french people to vote her or him into office?  Possibly,  but the presidential election in France is one person, one vote as opposed to the electoral college system in the US, so hopefully, sanity will prevail.

comments.name: Fruminous Bear
comments.body:
“She’s got far more political assets than Bardella,” Professor Marlière is quoted as saying. “ She’s been around for so long.” 

In fact,that's precisely her problem. Bardella is 30; Mme Le Pen will turn 58 next month. She indeed has been around for a long time, having become something of a shopworn figure in French politics. Sure, the RN faithful will vote for her. But they will vote for any RN flag-bearer, no matter who it is. 

But does Mme Le Pen have the wider appeal needed to win?  As an all-too-known quantity, she will have difficulty attracting votes from what the French call 'la droite fréquentable' -- 'the respectable right'.  In contrast, the pro-business, telegenic Bardella would very likely have had that broader appeal. 

In sum, Professor Marlière's view of Mme Le Pen's 'assets' is highly contestable. Her decision to run, thereby sidelining Bardella, is good news for all who fear an RN presidential victory.

By not consulting medical researchers about the potential scientific value of these collections, The New York Times presented an incomplete discussion of the history, ethics, and possible utility of preserving hair samples. While this article’s focus on the inclusion of hair samples taken from Native peoples as part of the hundreds of thousands of museum artifacts that remain at public and private museums is meritorious, most readers don’t understand the larger context: that it is **36 years** since NAGRPA (Native American Graves and Remains Repatriation Act) was passed, and only a portion of the artifacts have been legally returned to their closest descendants.

Every year that a museum delays repatriating items stolen from Natives is a year when more elders – who often are the only remaining knowledge-holders of critical cultural details about the artifacts — die, and the repatriation task for everyone becomes more difficult.

It is impossible to underestimate the profound grief and frustration felt by every one of the 575 federally-acknowledged Tribes and the hundreds of yet-to-be-acknowledged Tribal communities over these ongoing injustices.

There is a difference between film music, which is heard in the background, and classical music, which needs to meet all its artistic strength with music alone. In an article in the most recent Weekend Magazine, the author made multiple references to "culturally relevant" music. How insulting to those who are devoting their lives to making great and serious art. But I suppose this is what the author meant: POPULAR music. Popular music is fine and entertaining and necessary. And I love a lot of it. But it is not the same as classical music, which seeks to make sophisticated narrative statements through sound. The US is in a long-term and pretty rapid cultural decline when it comes to many art forms, including classical music. The solution is not to continue to dumb things down. The solution is very simple: comprehensive music education and a national commitment to valuing serious art of all kinds. I wish I could read something in the NY Times that talked about serious musical art, but I can't. It's not "culturally relevant." Guess what? Life, especially in 2026, is way more complicated than this kind of music. Art is not made to "soothe" you!

Every structural steel project undergoes changes during the detailing process; erection and shop plans are the final finish product, not the Engineer's design drawings. 

It's a complex process where senior drafts-people submit questions to the Engineer regarding steel design plan discrepancies, and then the Engineer provides the solutions.  Then the shop detail drawings are submitted for approval - every beam, every column and brace detailed out with all the connections, welds and bolts. the Engineer reviews each drawing and stamps their approval or lists the required changes and requests the drawings be resubmitted before fabrication begins. 

Hard to believe, in this age of computer modeling and stress analysis, that they built a structural 3D engineering model from the original steel erection plans and shop details and suffered this kind of structural failure.

While you may be angry at Russia's war on Ukraine and think, as a result, that these attacks are justified, you would be very naive to expect Russia to refrain from counterattacks against ALL parties involved. comments.body:

And an idea that NATO is poorly positioned to respond, perhaps without playing into Russian rhetoric that the Ukraine war is really a full-scale war with NATO?

That might then be used to justify mobilization of a larger number of Russian citizens.

comments.name: stephan morrow

I had a background in appreciation of modern art as far back as a naive Stuyvesant H.S. student where MOMA's cafe was our candy store to hang out in after school. Can't explain it & never ran across many fellow Stuyvesantians there. Strictly a solo trip but I didn't mind. I even, dare I say, became a self-appointed docent when a group of people ended up in front of a painting: I was off to the races. (the level of ignorance of so many attendees was impressive - even younger ones who just wanted to be photographed in front of a canvas. ) Anyway, in my year at The Freshman Grad Division: an experimental program where the most naive students were given graduate faculty to see what the combination would produce - I ran across Marcia Tucker - as an art history lecturer and she ushered myself and other lucky acolytes into a deeper appreciation of classical art: all the greats - Botticelli,Titian,   Rembrandt (striking anecdote was how @ 62 he had married his 14 yr old maid - after he had lost his fame & fortune.). But we stayed in touch & became good friends. Really. So one day we were crossing Forty Deuce & the pavement was wet & reflecting the red & green traffic lights: Me: "So is that art?". She "Yes. Why not? What defines art or beauty for that matter?". And on and on. So it's interesting how that question (brought up here) lingers still. 
My question now is "But 'is it great?' e.g. banana peels. (Skeptical. Will it be worshipped 20 yrs from now?) 
Art Dir
Grt Am Play Series

comments.name: WorldWatcher
comments.body: I'm the international coordinator for a large network of Congolese NGOs, most working on human rights, development and rule of law. A number of our organizations are involved in the Ebola response. We're trying to collaborate with the health authorities in the zones under government control, and fly under the radar in the zones under military occupation. Community members are so traumatized after many years of violence, occupation, and abandonment by their own government and the international community, that they have a hard time trusting the advice and actions of authorities - especially outsiders. This leads to attacks against the medical facilities and workers. We are doing what we can to gently explain how the virus works and what is needed to get it stopped. This is as much a psycho-social crisis as a medical crisis.

And in the case of the Antarctic Ice Sheet, regarding the marine based ice which is very sensitive to ocean temperatures—West Antarctica 3.3 meters of sea level rise equivalent of ice, East Antarctica 19 meters—we are committed to some response of the ice sheet to the heat that has already gone into the ocean. At 3°C, tens of meters eventually.

Times scales are the big question and the community in general has been conservative with time scales.
